#190057. Latest Update: The 10 Best Fitness Trackers, Tested by Our Fitness and Tech Experts

📅 15 Mar 2024 • ⏱️ 22m • 📚 Deep Dive (4322 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Menshealth ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: The 10 Best Fitness Trackers, Tested by Our Fitness and Tech Experts

📅 15 Mar 2024 | ⏱️ 22 min read (4322 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Menshealth

⏱️ ~22 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • NOT SURE WHAT fitness tracker is right for you?
  • Sources indicate that on the most basic level, the best fitness trackers offer GPS connectivity to help you stay on your training course and basic activity tracking.
  • Depending on what your health and fitness goals are (like losing weight, improving your sleep, or cutting time off your mile PR), the best fitness trackers can help you identify where your training is lacking, optimize your stress levels, improve your recovery time, and streamline your training sessions and daily wellness habits.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

NOT SURE WHAT fitness tracker is right for you? You've come to the right place. We've been wearing and documenting fitness trackers as far back as 2015, when we reviewed the very first Apple Watch. We started cross-comparing fitness trackers as early as 2017, when we broke down the best fitness trackers for activities like strength training, running, hiking, golf, and more. Now in 2026, we're more dialed into the state of fitness trackers than ever before as nearly all our editors are wearing some sort of device on a daily basis.

Sources indicate that on the most basic level, the best fitness trackers offer GPS connectivity to help you stay on your training course and basic activity tracking. Newer iterations of fitness trackers include advanced smartwatches that can do anything from tracking your archery workout to detecting a heart attack, as well as (our personal favorite) smart rings. Smart rings pack a ton (no literally, an absurd amount) of sleep/stress stats and workout/health information into a tiny package you wear on your finger 24/7.

Depending on what your health and fitness goals are (like losing weight, improving your sleep, or cutting time off your mile PR), the best fitness trackers can help you identify where your training is lacking, optimize your stress levels, improve your recovery time, and streamline your training sessions and daily wellness habits.

According to recent reports, as the Fitness and Reviews Editor at Men’s Health, it’s my job to test the latest and greatest fitness trackers. I am supported in this effort by my fellow editors like Fitness Director Ebenezer Samuel, C.S.C.S., Grooming Editor Sean Zucker, Senior Gear Editor Ryan Brower, and Senior Fitness Editor Brett Williams, NASM. We have put countless fitness trackers through the gauntlet and evaluated models on accuracy, design, durability, and price. We also paid close attention to comfort, ease of use, syncing with our favorite apps, and their ability to meet our standards for any activity.

We upgrade our lineup of fitness trackers often, so you can expect up-to-date information that takes into account the latest fitness tracker releases.

Industry observers note that if you want a basic level fitness tracker, the Whoop PEAK membership with its latest 5.0 band may be your answer. Men’s Health Fitness Director Ebenezer Samuel, C.S.C.S. backs this device for that reason. “Simplicity is what works here, because it's reliable, has great battery life, and I don't need to think about it,” he claims. The Whoop 5.0 Band is a fitness tracker band, which means though it’s still decently functional, it does not have a display like most wrist devices. It tracks all of your data in the corresponding phone app, but it’s worth noting, you cannot see the data directly on your wrist.

If you like the no-frills appearance, the Whoop 5.0 can definitely accomplish most of your tracking needs. “Whoop's activity sensing has improved over the years and continues to take steps,” says Samuel. It can track anything from running, cycling, and rowing to weightlifting, yoga, soccer, and even massage therapy. From our personal experience with Whoop, we love how it fits on the wrist. It is one of the more comfortable fitness trackers we’ve worn—the strap has a soft back, is woven with microfilament yarn, and can also be easily adjusted.

Recent findings suggest that unfortunately, Samuel had some qualms with the heart rate monitoring. “The device isn't tremendously accurate in terms of tracking heart rate, which is important to note,” he says. “In general, note that whatever [Whoop] is telling you about heart rate, it's almost always overshooting.” This can be an matter because a lot of the other tracking metrics (calories, activity, etc.) are based around heart rate. However, if you just want something basic to wear on your wrist, count your steps, and give you a general look into your health and workouts, Whoop 5.0 Band with the Peak membership will do just that.

Industry observers note that read More: Garmin Vs. Apple Watch.

Oura was a pioneer in the smart ring space, and it’s still the best smart ring we’ve tested to date (and we’ve tested a lot). Multiple editors have been wearing an Oura Ring for the last ten years and can attest that each latest iteration outkicks the competition. This particular release updated a few physical features: Oura shifted to a fully titanium build (vs. a titanium exterior, epoxy interior), added smaller and larger sizes, and ditched its three-nodule sensor design. This latest model eliminates the nodules that used to be on the inside of the ring and pinch into my finger on the Oura Ring 3. Those aren't required anymore with the new tech, so that is a huge improvement over the past model.

It has been revealed that the battery can also last up to eight days now, instead of just seven. And the updated software is available on all models, latest and old. While Oura has always offered heart rate monitoring, the new software now features automatic heart rate monitoring, allowing you to detect and track your workout stats without hitting the “Record HR workout” button. This automatic detection feature also lends itself to workout monitoring for over 40 activities (a new capability compared to the past, solely cardio-focused tracking that Oura offered).

The daytime stress features have also gotten an improvement—one of our favorites is illness detection. The Oura Ring 5 can detect changes in your stress stats and body temperature that may indicate an illness before you feel the entirety of the symptoms. A couple of months ago, one editor felt a slight earache when they woke up, and Oura called out they may have a cold coming on. The next day, that cold had arrived. It’s not always entirely accurate like this—there have been a few times the Oura Ring has said we were getting sick when it was actually just a hangover (oops).

Even as Oura lovers, we’d be remiss not to call out one of the downsides to the product: In order to attain full use of the Oura Ring, you need to pay a monthly subscription fee of $5.99 (or $69.99 per year). There are other smart rings in the space that don’t require any fee (shout out to our second favorite product, the Ultrahuman ring), but with the updated technology and consistent top-of-the-line features, we deem the extra $69.99 per year a pretty minimal price to pay.

For the most style-conscious people, the tech giant also released a Ceramic version of the Oura Ring 4, which offers a unique look and additional color options.

Read More: Our Hands-On Test of the Oura Ring 5.

Adventurers, look this way. We’re not exaggerating when we say this is the most rugged fitness tracker we have tested. The Garmin Instinct 3 AMOLED is packed with technology and has a thick face made for trail hikes, rock climbing, and even swimming (it’s water rated up to 100 meters). According to Men’s Health contributor Korin Miller, this Garmin can take a beating. “I accidentally banged it into several doorways and even scraped it against a kettlebell during a clumsy gym moment—it still looks brand fresh,” Miller states.

Recent findings suggest that in addition to its outwardly masculine look and durable design, the technology here is super simple to navigate, which can’t be said for all fitness trackers. Though there’s no touchscreen, Miller had the five buttons figured out within just a few minutes of receiving the product. And while you can track up to 30 different workout types, Miller praises the display for the easy-to-digest layout outside of workout mode. “The 390-by-390-pixel AMOLED display resolution is sharp and bright, allowing Garmin to jam a lot of stats on the home screen. At a glance, you can see your step count, heart rate, weather, date, time, and more. It’s arranged smartly in a way to deliver plenty of information without feeling overwhelming,” she claims.

Industry observers note that but one of our favorite features? Garmin prioritizes a wind-down time, switching from a jam-packed interface to just a clock during the time you are typically sleeping (which you note during set-up). It’s worth mentioning that in order to be this rugged and durable, the Garmin Instinct 3 is also quite heavy at 53 grams. But if you’re going hard on the trails, there’s no better wrist partner.

Read More: Our Hands-On Test of the Garmin Instinct 3.

In a recent development, at this cost, you’d expect a simple appearance, no touchscreen, and limited functionality. However, the Google Pixel Watch 5 has a beautiful, easy-to-navigate touchscreen, a smooth design, and almost all the metrics you’d get on a more high-end device.

Sources indicate that google puts a substantial emphasis on overall wellness rather than just fitness tracking, focusing on breathing and stress management. “This is a very underrated device and it's gotten more accurate with the third edition,” indicates Samuel. “The breathing exercises don't reinvent the wheel, but the presentation is solid and the timing is good. Overall, in this market, there's a lot we don't fully understand about stress levels, and some of the algorithms are simplistic. But Google has smartly gotten us thinking about how we feel, and that's a good thing.”.

If this watch tracks stress, readiness, and sleep, what are the limitations of this budget-friendly device? Well, it doesn’t offer as many workout modes as most other fitness trackers, clocking in at just 41 options. You also have to charge it every day, and it’s only compatible with Android devices. But for such a clean, aesthetic appearance and great individual wellness metrics, we definitely consider this fitness tracker a steal.

Sources indicate that most fitness trackers carry a hefty price tag, so if you’re in the market but not looking to sell out on this particular accessory, the Suunto Race S is the best value you’ll find. With a high definition AMOLED touchscreen, over 95 sport modes, and a water rating up to 50m, the specs here are just as good as you’ll find on many high-end fitness trackers. The AMOLED display on this watch is fantastic for its compact design. And personally, I think the Suunto Race S is superior to the larger model.

A lot of fitness trackers in this price range (around $350) offer only more basic tracking, like steps and calories burned. That’s not the case here, there is more to this fitness watch than just a run tracker—there are workouts and other great fitness insights, like HRV, sleep monitoring, activity tracking and race pacing. Sure, it's not as powerful as a top-of-the-line Garmin, but it gets the job done and brings great value.

Recent findings suggest that let’s chat about some of those features. Sleep tracking is having a moment and the Suunto Race S can track your sleep duration, timing, deep sleep, light sleep, heart rate, REM and HRV from sleep. One downside here? Wearing a watch to bed isn’t for everyone. Another cool feature worth digging into is race pacing. If you’re training for an upcoming marathon (or just life), the Race Pacer can help keep you on track when the mid-long run rut strikes. Overall, this is a great budget-friendly find—just note that if you opt for the titanium version over the stainless steel version, that will hike the price up by $120 (which makes it not as budget-friendly).

It has been revealed that apple fans already know how great the Apple Watch Ultra 4 is. It features a large, durable aerospace-grade titanium body built for outdoor adventure. It’s water-rated up to 100m and boasts dual-frequency GPS. What’s that do for you exactly? It offers much more accurate tracking in tough environments (like densely populated cities, mountain terrain, and forests)—great for trail runners and climbers.

Apple has always been at the top of the game for fitness tracking. The Ultra 4 offers all the typical metrics of the older Apple Watch models—activity rings, over 60 workout modes, blood oxygen, ECG, etc. But the Ultra 4 can be used as a dive computer, an emergency siren, and a compass that retraces your steps (ideal for those prone to getting lost mid-hike).

It has been revealed that A watch that can do this much won’t look dainty on the wrist, though. Men’s Health Senior Fitness Editor Brett Williams, NASM wrapped everything up nicely here. “The newly introduced design overhauled the sensor, which is on the rear of the watch and sits against the wearer’s wrist. Even though the casing is still the same 49-millimeter size as previous versions of the device and the sensor takes up the same amount of space.” Williams continues, “There’s now more surface area for device-to-skin contact for ECG readings, a new, circular optical sensing array, and larger, more efficient LEDs for heart rate sensing.”.

For us, the only real downside is that it’s a bit chunky on the wrist, but we’ll take it—the Apple Watch Ultra 4 is truly the full package for all iPhone people.

Read More: Our Hands-On Test of the Apple Watch Ultra 4.

Recent findings suggest that if you’ve ever been significant into running, you’ve likely considered a Garmin watch. But the Garmin Fēnix 9 isn’t just great for run tracking—it tracks over 100 different types of workouts and can last up to 29 days on one charge. In addition to its functionality, the Garmin Fēnix 9 also boasts a high-end design. One of the thinner offerings in the way of chunky Garmins, this is the perfect fitness tracking watch for anyone who doesn’t want to wear anything too cumbersome on the wrist (plus it now comes in a 43mm size). This watch has everything that fitness tracking powerhouse Garmin has to offer packed into its low-profile casing.

Industry observers note that one of the coolest offerings? Garmin has both an AMOLED and a solar-powered option. The solar-powered watch can extend the battery life even further, but the screen is not quite as bright as the AMOLED option. The solar watch also does not have a touchscreen like the AMOLED one, making it a bit less convenient to have to click through the features via buttons.

While the Garmin Fēnix 9 has the capabilities to track pretty much any metric you want tracked, the charging experience falls a bit short. While the battery can last up to 24 days in low-power mode, turning on GPS drops that to just under 24 hours of charge—a stark difference. Additionally, the charging cord is a bit short, so you might want to keep these USB-C charger extension cords on hand to charge your Garmin.

Industry observers note that overall, this is a sleek, all-in-one package with a unique (and modern) solar-powered option. If you don’t mind a bit of a sub-par charging experience, you can’t get more premium than the Garmin Fēnix 9.

Recent findings suggest that no iPhone? No problem. The Galaxy Watch9 can go anywhere thanks to a large scratch-resistant screen and a strong titanium case. One of our favorite features is the advanced sleep coaching that analyzes your sleep habits, suggests what you can do to improve, and is even FDA-approved to detect sleep apnea. We also appreciate the body composition reader—in just a few seconds, the Galaxy Watch9 works to tell you your vitals, and even provides a body fat estimate. These stats are prone to inaccuracy (few home devices can accurately track body fat), but we give props to Samsung for trying to push metrics to another level.

Sources indicate that the Galaxy Watch9 also delivers the features you expect in high-end smartwatches. That means accurate dual-frequency GPS specs and voice navigation. Nailing these (as Samsung does) is extra-critical, partly because the Galaxy Watch9 has some new competition for Android consumers (namely, from Google's Pixel Watch).

Thanks to several generations of trial and error and latest AI health insights, the Galaxy Watch gets the edge as our preferred pick for Android owners. There are more health insights and data in this watch than most competitors. Once you grant the device access to your health insights on your phone, it will make recommendations on sleep, exercise, and overall health, after you choose what your own personal goals are. I appreciate the design as well, which looks more like a classic watch than other smartwatch options.

The array of features available and the materials used to craft the watch have been optimized a few times over, thus producing a seriously strong, long-lasting fitness tracker (and everyday smart watch) most users will be happy adding to their training arsenal.

Read More: The Best Smartwatches.

It has been revealed that when you’re just starting out, you probably want a no-fuss fitness tracker to help get your bearings. The G-Shock Move is easy to navigate and offers just enough tracking to get you started. Men’s Health Grooming and Commerce Editor Sean Zucker tested it out for himself and likes how easy it is for newbies. “Thankfully, where the watch really excels is where it’s most meant to be used—when you’re working out or going for a run,” Zucker says. “Its face has a simple design and navigating it was a breeze, even for someone as technologically challenged as myself. It was easy to switch between lap/route times, heart rate/zone, homepage, etc. while I was running with only a couple of clicks (the watch itself only has 4 buttons so I appreciate the simplified design).”.

Recent findings suggest that the G-Shock Move tracks all your basic needs: steps, running, walking, heart rate, blood oxygen, and even sleep recovery. Zucker also found it quite comfortable. “[It’s a] super comfortable watch, and handles sweat/rain with ease,” he indicates. “It doesn’t move around at all or get greasy after a long run/workout.” Though he did have a couple qualms with the functionality.

Recent findings suggest that “Now, I’m not someone who likes to wear a watch, let alone a fitness watch, all of the time but I will if I have a few minutes or I’m planning out a run,” notes Zucker. “I’ll check in on what I’ve done that week and unfortunately, the app doesn’t let you access any of that info unless your phone is right now connected, which is, in my professional opinion, quite annoying.” Another small downside, Zucker did mention he had a tough time with initial setup.

“It’s notable to note that I am generally 100 years old and grumpy about this type of stuff, [but] still, the set up on this watch was a bit of a pain,” states Zucker. “There were a lot of ads (this extends to the app itself after you start using as well, very muddy).” If you can get past the setup and are okay with only being able to check past stats when you’re connected to the phone app, this is a great beginner-friendly tracker offering all the basic functions you need to kick off your fitness tracking journey.

Fitbit is back, with a vengeance. The Fitbit Air is the brand’s smallest and lightest tracker ever, weighing just 12 grams and featuring a design 25 percent smaller than the discontinued Luxe. Setup is simple through the upcoming Google Health app, and the Air’s tracking features, including 24/7 heart rate, HRV, skin temperature, and sleep, run seamlessly in the background, with automatic workout detection and a reliable seven-day battery life.

What truly elevates the experience is the integration of Google’s Health Coach AI, available through a Google Health Premium subscription, which is included for those who already have Google One. Food logging is a surprise standout—you can snap a picture of your meal, and the app accurately breaks down the macros. While the core tracking functions are available without a subscription, the real value comes from the Premium features like AI coaching, deeper analytics, and adaptive plans. But you don’t need the membership for the basic features.

Industry observers note that some trade-offs to consider: The Air is screenless, so you can’t check notifications or your heart rate on the go, which may take some getting used to for smartwatch consumers. The default band can feel a bit stiff, and you charge it off-wrist. Still, the Fitbit Air is a compelling option for those who want minimalist, screenless health tracking without a hefty commitment.

At $99 with no required subscription, it’s an accessible entry point for anyone who wants comprehensive health data and a genuinely helpful AI coach, especially those seeking a distraction-free, streamlined alternative to full-featured smartwatches.

Read More: Our Full Review of the Google Fitbit Air.

Fitness trackers started as mostly wrist devices—from step counters like the Fitbit to the original Apple Watch. Now, you can choose from an array of fitness tracking watches or smart rings, all of which track far more than just your fitness. While most of these devices offer similar capabilities, the design you choose—watch or ring—will depend on your own personal aesthetic.

Industry observers note that do you prefer the look of a fitness tracker watch? Do you find it more convenient to navigate all your stats on your wrist? Or do you like the look of a ring better and prefer the sleeker, more compact design? If so, are you also agreeable to the fact that you will need to visit your phone app to view all of your stats? Only you have the answers to these personal questions.

Fitness trackers don’t just track fitness anymore. Sure, your workouts are still a key part of what these devices do, but in addition they’re also tracking your sleep, heart rhythm patterns, blood oxygen levels, HRV, stress, and even caffeine consumption. Fitness trackers are more of an overall wellness tool than ever before.

That mentioned, the type of fitness tracker you choose should weigh heavily on the way you intend to use it. If you’re just looking for insights into your sleep cycle, you’ll probably want a smart ring that’s fairly comfortable to wear to bed each night. If you’re training for a marathon, you may want a watch with a touchscreen that’s easy to navigate mid-run. This last part may be especially vital: If you’re already using certain tracking apps that you love (let’s say, Apple Fitness for instance), you’ll want to make sure you find yourself a fitness tracker that is compatible with that app in particular.

The accuracy of a fitness tracker begins and ends with how precisely it tracks your heart rate (most other stats, with the exception of fresh hydration tracking features, are derived from this baseline data). This mark is as much about pure accuracy as it is about consistency of accuracy, which is key in helping you understand your own fitness trends. While some trackers tend to be more accurate than others, all of the trackers we included here were consistently accurate.

In a recent development, with the exception of the Apple Watch Ultra 4 and the Samsung Galaxy Watch9 (two fitness trackers that are equal parts smartwatch but have seen improvement in their battery life), the fitness trackers we tested are all designed to run for days (even weeks) on a single charge. We love a fitness tracker that needs minimal charging, and we also love a fitness tracker that can run for a long time when running its GPS mode. Two fitness trackers that surprised us when testing battery life include the Suunto Race S (up to 13 days on a single charge) and the Garmin Instinct 3 (21 days on a single charge when set to its most basic mode).

According to recent reports, all fitness trackers are made to take a beating, but some are better designed than others. Look at case construction, screen construction, and for smart rings, material. The most advanced fitness trackers (smart rings included) are typically made with stainless steel, titanium, or another type of quality metal. For screens, sapphire glass is a premium spec to look for thanks to its high scratch resistance and strength.

Recent findings suggest that sometimes the most durable fitness tracker is unnecessary, though, especially if you are using it for pavement running. In fact, a plastic construction fitness tracker can be a much better choice for cardio-intensive activities like running and biking, since the material is going to be much lighter than stainless steel or titanium. On the flip side, if you are using your fitness tracker for strength training (or hiking or trail running), it would make sense to look for stronger materials.

#190056. Tesla on Autopilot/FSD hit an overturned truck at 71 mph, killing 3

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1489 w)
📖 Baca
EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Electrek ↗ Open Full Page

Tesla on Autopilot/FSD hit an overturned truck at 71 mph, killing 3

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1489 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A Tesla Model 3 drove into an overturned box truck on I-75 near Naples, Florida, killing two of its passengers and a man who had stopped to help.
  • Sources indicate that police and local media covered the May 31 crash as a truck wreck in the dark, and none of it mentioned a driver-assist system.
  • It has been revealed that just before 4 a.m.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A Tesla Model 3 drove into an overturned box truck on I-75 near Naples, Florida, killing two of its passengers and a man who had stopped to help. Tesla’s own report to federal regulators indicates Autopilot or “Full Self-Driving” was engaged, at 71 mph.

Sources indicate that police and local media covered the May 31 crash as a truck wreck in the dark, and none of it mentioned a driver-assist system. It’s the latest case in our ongoing investigation into fatal crashes hidden in Tesla’s NHTSA data, and it lands as Tesla’s monthly crash count hits another record.

It has been revealed that just before 4 a.m. on Sunday, May 31, 2026, the 31-year-old driver of a 2014 Freightliner lost the road near the Pine Ridge Road exit in Collier County, steered back onto southbound I-75, and flipped it, according to the Florida Highway Patrol. The overturned truck ended up blocking the center and outside lanes.

Recent findings suggest that jonathan Garcia Arias, a 25-year-old Naples man and former Marine, was driving by in a BMW. He pulled over and got out to help the truck driver.

Then a southbound 2023 Tesla with five young men from Naples inside came up on the scene. FHP’s report says the front of the Tesla hit the underside of the overturned truck and Garcia Arias. Two of the Tesla’s passengers, aged 18 and 19, died at the scene, and Garcia Arias died later in the hospital. The 20-year-old driver and two more passengers were seriously hurt.

A few days later, FHP used the crash as a warning about stopping near wrecks on the interstate. Senior Trooper Kenn Watson said the Tesla driver would have seen only the truck’s underside, with “no lights, no reflectors, nothing warning them.”.

It has been revealed that so that’s the official story. A dark obstacle, a driver who couldn’t see it in time. Nobody stated a word about Autopilot.

Industry observers note that under NHTSA’s Standing General Order, automakers have to report crashes where a Level 2 driver-assist system was engaged within 30 seconds of impact and someone was killed or hurt. Tesla filed one for this crash.

It identifies the car as a 2023 Model 3 on a highway, flags a traffic incident on the roadway, and marks the automation “Engagement Status” as “Verified Engaged.” That means Tesla confirmed through its own telematics that Autopilot or FSD was on. It logs a pre-crash speed of 71 mph and a fatality, lists the Florida Highway Patrol as the investigating agency, and says it learned of the crash from police and the media.

Then it blacks out the crash narrative, the software version, and whether the road was within the system’s approved operating domain, all as “confidential business information.” That’s the same redaction Tesla applies to 99.9% of its reports.

It has been revealed that the report also surfaced late. Tesla filed it as a 5-Day report, the urgent category for fatal crashes, but it didn’t land until Tesla’s September filings, more than three months after the crash. And Tesla lists law enforcement as one of the ways it found out about it.

Recent findings suggest that how we matched it: Tesla logged the incident time as 07:56 UTC, which converts to 3:56 a.m. in Florida, two minutes off the 3:54 a.m. in FHP’s report. The city, the highway, the 2023 model year, the month and the fatal outcome all line up, and it’s the only fatal Tesla driver-assist report in Naples that month. It’s the same crash.

According to recent reports, A Tesla on driver-assist going highway speed into the underside of a significant truck, in the dark, in Florida. If that sounds familiar, it should.

In 2016, Joshua Brown was killed near Williston when his Model S on Autopilot drove under a tractor-trailer crossing the highway. In 2019, Jeremy Banner died in Delray Beach when his Model 3 on Autopilot went under a trailer at 68 mph and had its roof sheared off. In both crashes, neither the driver nor the system braked.

In a recent development, trooper Watson’s point was that a human couldn’t see the truck. But a major, unlit obstacle sitting across two lanes at night is exactly the kind of thing a driver-assist system is supposed to catch, and Tesla now sells FSD as nearly ready to drive with nobody watching. And an attentive driver could clearly see it, as the BMW driver did, and stop before the Tesla arrived.

Industry observers note that we want to be fair about what the data doesn’t prove. “Engaged within 30 seconds” is the reporting trigger. Tesla’s 71 mph may be a telematics snapshot rather than the impact speed. And with the software version redacted, we can’t say whether this was Autopilot or FSD.

The NHTSA release that surfaced this crash, covering filings through October 15, also set a upcoming monthly high. Tesla reported 264 driver-assist crashes in September 2026, beating July’s 236, which was itself a record. That’s up from 135 in March.

September may still grow as late reports come in. This Naples crash shows how late they can be.

Our merged dataset now holds 4,669 Tesla driver-assist crash reports since 2019, 69 of them flagged fatal. The same release added two other fatal reports, both “Verified Engaged” and both covered locally with no mention of driver-assist: a Model Y that hit a tree and burned in El Dorado Hills, California, killing three, and a Model X that hit a signal pole in Naples on September 30, killing a passenger. We’ll lay those out separately.

Three people died on I-75, including a man who got out of his car to help a stranger. Tesla knows its driver-assist was on, knows the speed, holds the telematics, and filed a federal report saying so. Then it sealed everything that would explain what the car did, and the public got a story about a dark truck.

That's what happens when the system has to identify all objects in the camera frame before it can start to estimate the objects position and then relative distance and then relative velocity. Unrecognizable objects will destroy all your logic. This is a design failure and not something Tesla can actually fix.

Industry observers note that compare that to radars and lidars that directly measure distances and relative velocities of everything in front of the car, regardless of what it is. That is a far better approach because you do not want the car the impact objects on its trajectory regardless of what those objects turn out to be.

Tesla’s whole pitch for FSD is that the car sees better than you do, and yet, Tesla vehicles on Autopilot and FSD keep crashing on stationary objects on the highway. It’s the same failure that killed Joshua Brown and Jeremy Banner years ago. If the system saw the truck and the driver overrode it, Tesla should say so. It was quick to do that in the Katy crash when the data helped it. If the system didn’t see it, that’s a safety defect regulators and owners need to know about.

Either way, the redaction protects Tesla, not the people on the road. It’s the same pattern we found in Vineland and in July’s four fatal crashes, and the crash count keeps setting records.

Recent findings suggest that we’re asking the Florida Highway Patrol for the full crash report, whether its investigators got Tesla’s raw vehicle data, and whether they even knew the system was engaged. If they didn’t, the only party that knows what this car did is the one that sealed the file.

#190055. Industry News: Walking, Yoga, or Zumba? Which Exercises Help Relieve Menopause Mood Symptoms

📅 17 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (738 w)

Industry News: Walking, Yoga, or Zumba? Which Exercises Help Relieve Menopause Mood Symptoms

📅 17 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (738 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Physical activity may help support mood and improve quality of life during the menopause transition, according to a study published on October 13 in Menopause, the journal of the Menopause Society.
  • This review of 12 clinical trials involving over 1,000 people ages 40 to 65 found that both aerobic and mind-body exercises may be associated with reduced depressive symptoms and improved well-being.
  • It is common for individuals to experience psychological symptoms during menopause, including depression, anxiety, low mood, stress, and difficulty with thinking and memory.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Physical activity may help support mood and improve quality of life during the menopause transition, according to a study published on October 13 in Menopause, the journal of the Menopause Society.

This review of 12 clinical trials involving over 1,000 people ages 40 to 65 found that both aerobic and mind-body exercises may be associated with reduced depressive symptoms and improved well-being.

It is common for individuals to experience psychological symptoms during menopause, including depression, anxiety, low mood, stress, and difficulty with thinking and memory. These symptoms can have a significant effect on quality of life, with an estimated 1 in 10 women leaving work due to menopause symptoms.

This study found that regular physical activity may help improve certain psychological symptoms and overall quality of life during menopause.

The types of physical activity in the review were broken into two categories: aerobic-based exercise (ABIs) and mind-body activities (MBAs).

Sources indicate that the researchers found that ABIs highlighted the strongest effects on reducing depressive symptoms and improving overall quality of life. This may be particularly relevant during perimenopause when women may be more vulnerable to mood instability due to estrogen fluctuations.

Sherry Ross, MD, board certified OB/GYN and Women’s Health Expert at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, who wasn’t involved in the study, pointed out that there are various ways that ABIs can have positive effects.

Ross explained that aerobic exercise may help improve menopausal symptoms through several mechanisms, including the release of endorphins, reduced inflammation, improved cholesterol levels, and better regulation of body temperature and sleep cycles.

MBAs were shown to have a greater effect on improving psychological quality of life. These exercises involve mindfulness, body awareness, and breathwork. They may help improve emotional regulation.

In a recent development, ABIs tended to require fewer sessions. This may mean these types of exercises are easier to fit in, especially if you are facing time or energy constraints. For example, in one trial, participants were instructed to walk for 30 minutes, three times per week. In another trial, participants attended three hour-long Zumba classes per week.

In contrast, one trial using MBAs instructed participants to attend two 75-minute yoga classes each week, and another had participants attend daily one-hour yoga classes.

Stephanie Faubion, MD, Director for the Mayo Clinic Center for Women’s Health and Medical Director for The Menopause Society, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that these findings are encouraging.

However, she also cautioned that this was a relatively small body of evidence. “While physical activity is an important component of a healthy lifestyle during midlife, I would be cautious about interpreting these findings to mean that exercise is a treatment for depression related specifically to menopause,” she mentioned.

Research has shown that physical activity can positively affect mental health. Studies have also found that regular exercise can help improve symptoms of depression and anxiety.

Faubion told Healthline that, broadly speaking, regular physical activity may support mood through multiple pathways, including better sleep, improved physical function, and overall well-being.

However, she also noted that this study cannot tell us precisely why the improvements occurred or whether aerobic exercise is superior to other forms of activity.

Faubion remarked that recommending physical activity during and after menopause extends well beyond mood.

“Physical activity is important for cardiovascular and metabolic health, maintaining muscle mass and physical function, and supporting bone health,” she noted.

“These become particularly key at midlife as women experience age- and menopause-related changes in body composition, bone, and cardiometabolic health,” Faubion added.

Ross agreed that physical activity is important for more than just mood and mental health improvement. She also noted that there are other types of exercise beyond ABIs and MBAs that can benefit people during menopause:.

“These types of activities help with weight loss or allow women to maintain a healthy weight. If you are not ready for aerobic exercises, stretching and simple exercises help with balance and stability,” Ross said.

Faubion told Healthline that physical activity is an vital part of healthy aging and should be encouraged during the menopause transition, but it should not be suggested that women can simply exercise their way out of significant depression or other bothersome menopause symptoms.

“Women experiencing persistent depression, anxiety, or symptoms that interfere with their quality of life should seek evaluation and discuss the full range of evidence-based treatment options with their healthcare clinician,” Faubion mentioned.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that when you’re trying to unwind at the end of a long day, turning on the “major light” is simply not the move. The glare of a way-too-bright overhead light is not only unflattering but oftentimes overstimulating. It can make your otherwise cozy bedroom feel more like a department-store dressing room, leaving relaxation a little bit harder to come by. The right bedroom lighting, on the other hand, can bring a sense of warmth, atmosphere, and visual interest to the space where you spend some of your most cherished downtime.

The secret lies in layered lighting, which involves a series of soft illumination sources working together in concert: A bedside lamp provides focused task lighting for reading, while wall sconces free up valuable nightstand space and introduce a soft diffused glow. Floor lamps can brighten an otherwise neglected corner, and a beautiful chandelier or pendant light doubles as a bedroom’s focal point, even when the light is switched off.

Recent findings suggest that dimmable fixtures and warm white light bulbs can be especially transformational in bedrooms that also function as an office or a hangout space. Ahead, we’ve rounded up our favorite bedroom lighting ideas, including sculptural statement pieces, portable table lamps, and wall-mounted fixtures that usher in a sense of calm.

In a recent development, for a reading nook, a work-from-home space, or just a little warm white lighting, a floor lamp can show off your taste without sacrificing functionality. We’ve pulled two designer-favorite must-haves for those in the world of interior design.

Sources indicate that this 1960s model from Danish designer Mads Caprani hasn’t gone out of style since its release. The pleated shade, bentwood spine, and U-shaped cast-iron base make it one of the most easily recognized and iconic designs in floor lamps to this day. Another lamp for tastemakers, this design from Isamu Noguchi has made the rounds in many celebrity home tours from a minimalist Brooklyn brownstone to Troye Sivan’s modern Melbourne home. Commerce director Rachel Fletcher has previously named a Noguchi lamp one of her bedroom essentials. The reputation of Noguchi’s work and the unique style of his Akari lamps make this a design staple for anyone hoping to cultivate a modern bedroom.

We love the look of dual table lamps to frame your bed and create a distinct visual space in your bedroom. It also allows your bed to feel like a conscious design choice instead of a strictly functional piece. We’re taking bedside lamp notes from this Portland home owned by the lead singer of The Shins and decorated by Jessica Helgerson. And, if you don’t want to do things matchy-matchy, any one of these lamps would look great solo too.

We love this moody metallic option from Article for a midcentury look—and we named it one of our favorite bedside lamps after ample editor testing. At $149, the price is also right.

The Flos Bellhop table lamp is a great source of ambient light in this minimalist Barcelona bedroom.

And, if you love the simple glass shape, they’re also available as wall sconces for a stylish outdoor lighting moment.

Wall lighting brings a warm dimension to the design of your bedroom and provides great task lighting for a bedtime read. Its distinctive arrangement of overlapping shades creates a sculptural silhouette, with each layer directing and diffusing light. Sources indicate that if you’re looking for guidance when it comes to your bedroom lights, it’s vital to keep a variety of factors in mind. Do you do a lot of reading in bed? Maybe table lamps should be your primary focus. Do you have enough fixtures to keep the space illuminated but not too bright? Perhaps a floor lamp or two will provide that glow for you. Women Aging Well: Lessons From Memories and Reflections

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (793 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 24, 2026 | Reviewed by Abigail Fagan.
  • In a recent development, in Tennessee, I walked a magnificent labyrinth inspired by a clock, formed with 1,000 feet of stone, designed as a space of reflection and connection.
  • According to recent reports, as I get older, I am more aware that the path in is never the same as the path out.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 24, 2026 | Reviewed by Abigail Fagan.

In a recent development, in Tennessee, I walked a magnificent labyrinth inspired by a clock, formed with 1,000 feet of stone, designed as a space of reflection and connection. The artist, Thea Alvin, titled her installation "Time for Love." Since I’ve been thinking about the importance of time as we age, I wandered slowly and quietly on the spiral path toward its center, open to whatever thoughts and feelings emerged. Immediately I relaxed, knowing I would arrive at the center, stay a while, and return along the same path.

According to recent reports, as I get older, I am more aware that the path in is never the same as the path out. No path is ever the same because of changes in weather, light, time of day, and the path itself. I am not the same. Just as we can never step in the same river twice, we can never walk along the same path because neither we nor the path remain the same. We evolve over time; as we age, we are continuously unfolding and hopefully, moving toward self-discovery and a center of calm.

Industry observers note that I experienced entering the labyrinth as an opportunity to be open and curious about my life at this moment. I have always been drawn to spiral shapes as they are often associated with evolution and transformation. As a nature lover, I notice spiral shapes of pinecones, sunflowers, and other life forms. As I walked the spiral path, I heard the wind, the birdsongs, and the crunching gravel underneath my feet. I listened deeply to myself, without judgment or criticism. When a thought or feeling surfaced, I attempted to observe it and see what it meant. I stayed with that thought and waited to see what else emerged. These were my mind’s musings as I walked to the center. Cultivating curiosity and willingness to stay with a thought or feeling as we age can help us deepen awareness about ourselves, our relationships, and hopefully, encourage us to examine the choices we make in our daily lives.

Recent findings suggest that at the center, I sat on a boulder under a Beech tree, contemplating "Time For Love." The structure was commissioned as a space for family members to come, sit, and remember their loved one who died. The place feels sacred. In my reflection, I recalled people and pets I’ve loved over the course of my life. I felt the warmth of those memories. I realized how much I enjoy reminiscing in this way; quietly, in nature, experiencing sadness and joy. As Thea Alvin intended, I was allocating "Time for Love." Noticing an internal shift, I recognized the necessity of giving myself this time for reflection on love. I needed to do this, and asked myself: How do I use my time compared to how I want to spend it?

Those questions stayed with me as I walked out of the labyrinth. I realized that this thought was not just inspired by the labyrinth but also by Varun Soni, Dean of Religious Life at USC, who spoke at a conference I attended about children and spirituality. He asked: “What deserves more of our attention?” “What would we like to make room for?” “What small change regarding our time could we make today?”.

Industry observers note that these are crucial questions to consider at any age; particularly when we are in our older years, when we are more aware of the time that has passed in relation to the time we may have ahead. The final question Dean Soni asked was “What can we do to change what we discover?” Sitting on a rock, under a tree, in the center of "Time for Love," I realized that I can dedicate time to feel the love that I had in my life, and to actively cultivate the love that I feel now. How will I make more time for love? I will remember those I loved; engage in activities I love, be with people I love, share love in ways that make others feel loved, and engage in acts of loving kindness.

Sources indicate that as I returned along the spiral path, I felt different. I was different. I discovered that actively engaging with love deserves more of my time and attention. And in making this change, I will feel this connection to love as a vital, positive force in my own aging.

#190051. Latest Update: Why Sleep Consistency May Be the Missing Piece When It Comes to Heart Health

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1745 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Womenshealthmag ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Why Sleep Consistency May Be the Missing Piece When It Comes to Heart Health

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1745 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Womenshealthmag

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that you probably already know that getting seven to nine hours of sleep each night is one of the best things you can do for your health and wellbeing.
  • It has been revealed that as it turns out, your heart might not be too happy about that.
  • Before you start stressing over every late night or weekend sleep-in, though, there's some crucial context to understand.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that you probably already know that getting seven to nine hours of sleep each night is one of the best things you can do for your health and wellbeing. But what happens if you’re consistently hitting that goal while going to bed at different times? Think 10 p.m. on Monday, midnight on Wednesday, and well past 1 a.m. on Saturday because it’s the weekend, after all.

It has been revealed that as it turns out, your heart might not be too happy about that. Upcoming research suggests that sleep consistency—which includes both when you go to bed and wake up, and how much sleep you get from night to night—could play an important role in cardiovascular health. And, while getting the recommended amount of shut-eye still matters, researchers are finding that how much your sleep fluctuates may deserve some attention, too.

Before you start stressing over every late night or weekend sleep-in, though, there's some crucial context to understand. Here's what the research actually found, why your body seems to care so much about routine, and how consistent your sleep schedule really needs to be.

Meet the experts: Nguyen Minh Tuan Viet, MD, PhD, is a neuroscientist and postdoctoral research fellow at Boston Children's Hospital and Harvard Medical School and lead researcher of the fresh study. Nour Makarem, PhD, is a cardiovascular epidemiologist in the department of epidemiology at Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health. Marie-Pierre St-Onge, PhD, is a professor of nutritional medicine and director of the Center of Excellence for Sleep & Circadian Research at Columbia University Irving Medical Center.

For the new study published in Circulation: Cardiovascular Quality and Outcomes, researchers analyzed more than one million nights of sleep data from 10,362 adults participating in the National Institutes of Health's All of Us Research Program, an initiative that aims to collect data from over one million Americans and create the country’s largest biomedical database.

Unlike previous studies that only looked at people's sleep habits for about a week, this one used about six months of Fitbit data to see how participants' bedtimes, wake-up times, and total sleep duration changed from night to night. They then compared those patterns with participants’ medical records and tracked their health for nearly four years.

In a recent development, the findings were pretty eye-opening: For every additional 29 minutes of variation in how long someone slept from night to night, their relative risk of serious heart problems, including heart attacks, heart failure, heart muscle disease, and certain strokes, was 24 percent higher. To be clear, that doesn't mean going to bed 29 minutes later than usual on a given night increases your heart disease risk by 24 percent. The researchers were looking at a statistical measure of how much someone's total sleep duration varied over time, rather than the consequences of one late bedtime. As of now, all this information does it point to a potential link between sleep schedule variation and heart disease.

Researchers also found that greater night-to-night fluctuations in bedtime and wake-up times were associated with a 23 percent and 20 percent higher relative risk of cardiovascular problems, respectively. This means that both the consistency of your sleep schedule and the consistency of the duration of that sleep may play a role in heart health.

Industry observers note that there are a few things worth keeping in mind, though. For starters, this study found a connection between inconsistent sleep and heart problems, but it couldn't prove that irregular sleep is what causes those problems. In fact, Viet points out that the relationship could work in the opposite direction too (i.e. early illness might actually make someone’s sleep more irregular). Plus, most participants were women and white, so we can't necessarily assume the findings apply to everyone. Still, the results add to growing evidence that sleep consistency deserves a place in the heart-health conversation.

In a recent development, your body has its own internal clock, known as your circadian rhythm, which determines when you're tired, when you're wide awake, and even how bodily functions like blood pressure and heart rate change throughout the day. And, it works at its best when it has a reasonably predictable schedule to follow. When you're constantly changing when you sleep and wake, you may disrupt that rhythm, a phenomenon known as circadian misalignment, explains Nour Makarem, PhD, a cardiovascular epidemiologist in the department of epidemiology at Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health.

Recent findings suggest that that disruption can impact some pretty vital cardiovascular processes, like how your body regulates blood pressure. Under normal circumstances, blood pressure usually drops by about 10 to 20 percent while you're sleeping to give your cardiovascular system a period of rest, but research by Makarem suggests that irregular sleep patterns may be associated with higher blood pressure and an increased risk of hypertension. “This is problematic because higher nocturnal blood pressure and having a non-dipping profile (blood pressure that does not dip or dip enough during sleep) are associated with higher risk for heart disease and stroke, the leading causes of death in women,” she says.

It has been revealed that your sleep schedule may also interact with other daily rhythms, including when you eat and exercise. These behaviors help regulate biological clocks throughout your body, including those involved in metabolism, Makarem claims. When those clocks fall out of sync, processes like blood sugar regulation may be affected, too. In fact, research has linked irregular sleep patterns with poorer glucose regulation and a higher risk of metabolic issues.

Industry observers note that research is still emerging, but scientists are noticing some notable links between sleep consistency and heart health. A 2025 study published in the Journal of Epidemiology & Community Health followed more than 72,000 adults and found that people with irregular sleep patterns had a higher risk of major cardiovascular events, including heart attacks and strokes. Another study published in Sleep in 2024 analyzed sleep patterns in more than 60,000 adults and found that sleep regularity was a stronger predictor of mortality risk than sleep duration in that population.

Recent findings suggest that so, does this mean having a consistent bed and rising time matters more than getting eight hours? Not necessarily. "The evidence for sleep regularity is rather nascent relative to that for sleep duration," states Marie-Pierre St-Onge, PhD, a professor of nutritional medicine and director of the Center of Excellence for Sleep & Circadian Research at Columbia University Irving Medical Center. She explains that while several studies have made the connection between irregular sleep and poorer health outcomes, more research needs to be done to determine whether making someone's sleep schedule more consistent can actually lower their cardiovascular risk. And, we do have plenty of evidence that getting enough sleep has positive affects on just about every system in the body, from brain function to muscle recovery.

Overall, there are still things researchers are learning about sleep consistency and heart health, but it’s safe to start thinking of it as another piece of the puzzle, alongside getting enough hours and making sure those hours are restorative.

Here's the million-dollar question: Does protecting your heart mean going to bed at exactly 10:30 p.m. every single night, no exceptions? Thankfully, no.

Sources indicate that ultimately, you’ve got some wiggle room. "In general, we would recommend that individuals try not to deviate by 60 min up or down from their average bedtime or sleep duration," states St-Onge, but the smaller the gap, the better.

It has been revealed that think of that as a target, not a hard-and-fast rule. An occasional late night or weekend sleep-in isn’t a reason to panic. What matters more is establishing a reasonably consistent pattern over a period of time rather than expecting yourself to follow a perfect schedule every single night.

It has been revealed that if you've had a particularly short night, St-Onge recommends trying to go to bed a little earlier and waking up a little later when your schedule allows, rather than trying to make up for all that lost sleep by sleeping in for hours. Most importantly, don't sweat it. "If one night is off, it's not all doom and gloom; you get right back on schedule the following night," states St-Onge.

Here are a few small changes experts recommend to improve your sleep routine without completely overhauling your lifestyle.

Before committing to being in bed every night by 9 p.m., consider what will actually make sense for your schedule. Earlier isn't automatically better. What's important is getting adequate sleep on a schedule that works with your body's natural rhythm and everyday responsibilities, explains St-Onge.

If your current bedtime is midnight but you'd ideally like to be asleep by 11, there's no need to make that change all at once. Makarem recommends gradually shifting your bedtime earlier by about 10 minutes each day until you reach your target. The idea is to give your body time to adjust rather than suddenly expecting yourself to fall asleep an hour earlier than usual.

It's tempting to stay up late on Friday and Saturday nights and make up for it by sleeping well into the morning, but even those brief changes can leave you feeling out of sync by the time Monday rolls around. If possible, St-Onge recommends keeping your weekend bedtimes within about an hour of your usual routine.

It has been revealed that if you wear an Apple Watch or Fitbit to bed, you know how easy it is to get caught up in the numbers. One morning you're celebrating a great sleep score, and the next you're wondering what went wrong because your tracker says you barely got any deep sleep.

Sources indicate that while these devices can be helpful for spotting patterns, the last thing you want is to start losing sleep over your sleep. Makarem recommends using trackers to keep tabs on your habits or remind you when it's time for bed, but only if they're actually helping. If checking your sleep stats is making you anxious, it's fine to ditch the data and simply pay attention to when you're going to bed and waking up.

And remember, you don't have to get your sleep schedule exactly right every single night to do something good for your heart. Small changes that you can actually stick with are worth more than chasing a perfect score. As Makarem puts it, "Progress is better than perfect.".

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A Tesla Model Y left a parkway in El Dorado Hills, California, hit a tree and burst into flames in September, killing three of the four people inside.
  • In a recent development, the crash was widely covered in the Sacramento area as a fiery single-car wreck.
  • According to recent reports, late on Saturday, September 12, 2026, a 2024 Tesla Model Y with four people inside was heading west on Serrano Parkway, between Terracina Drive and Silva Valley Parkway.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A Tesla Model Y left a parkway in El Dorado Hills, California, hit a tree and burst into flames in September, killing three of the four people inside. Tesla’s own report to federal regulators indicates Autopilot or “Full Self-Driving” was engaged, with the car doing 74 mph.

In a recent development, the crash was widely covered in the Sacramento area as a fiery single-car wreck. None of that coverage mentioned a driver-assist system. It’s the latest case in our ongoing investigation into fatal crashes hidden in Tesla’s NHTSA data.

According to recent reports, late on Saturday, September 12, 2026, a 2024 Tesla Model Y with four people inside was heading west on Serrano Parkway, between Terracina Drive and Silva Valley Parkway. That’s a residential part of the Serrano community in El Dorado Hills, east of Sacramento.

Recent findings suggest that according to the CHP’s Placerville office, the Model Y left the road “for unknown reasons,” hit a tree on the north side of the parkway, and caught fire. Officers got the call around 10:38 p.m. By the time they arrived, the car was fully engulfed in flames.

Charles Anthony Cameron, 30, of Sacramento, was thrown from the car and died at the scene. Alejandra Mendoza, 28, of Sacramento, and Kailauna Viola Mills, 28, of Roseville, were found dead inside once firefighters put out the fire. One of the two women was driving; CHP hasn’t publicly noted which.

Mills lived in Arizona and was visiting family. Her uncle told CBS Sacramento she worked in the medical field and was supposed to get married next April.

A fourth person, a 28-year-old Sacramento woman, survived with major injuries.

CHP says the cause is still under investigation. Speed, impairment, and how the car left the road haven’t been released. And nobody has said a word about Autopilot.

Under NHTSA’s Standing General Order, automakers have to report crashes where a Level 2 driver-assist system was engaged within 30 seconds of impact and someone is killed or hurt. Tesla filed a report on this one.

It lists a 2024 Model Y, a consumer vehicle, and marks the “Engagement Status” as “Verified Engaged.” That’s Tesla confirming through its own telematics that Autopilot or FSD was on. It logs a pre-crash speed of 74 mph, a fatality, and the California Highway Patrol as the investigating agency.

Then it redacts the narrative, the software version, and whether the road was inside the system’s operating domain, all as “confidential business information,” the same treatment Tesla gives 99.9% of its reports.

The rest of the report is strangely thin. Tesla lists the roadway type as “Unknown” and what the car hit as “Unknown,” even though police noted it was a tree. It checks only one source for how it learned of the crash: the media. So Tesla found out about a triple-fatal crash in one of its cars from the news, then went into its own data and confirmed its driver-assist was on.

How we matched it: Tesla logged the incident time as 05:36 UTC, which is 10:36 p.m. Pacific on September 12, within two minutes of the 10:38 p.m. call CHP responded to. The city, the 2024 Model Y, the month, and the fatal outcome all line up. It’s the only fatal Tesla driver-assist report from El Dorado Hills in the data. It’s the same crash.

According to recent reports, two of the three victims were found inside the car after the fire was out. The survivor got out of, or was pulled from, the wreckage, depending on the report.

CHP hasn’t remarked whether the doors played any role, and we’re not suggesting they did. But it’s a fair question to ask about any Tesla crash with a fire, now that NHTSA is writing newly introduced rules for emergency door releases after years of complaints about people getting trapped. We’ve asked.

Recent findings suggest that this is the second triple-fatal crash in Tesla’s latest NHTSA filings where its driver-assist was verified engaged and the public never heard about it. The other one was on I-75 in Naples. Add Vineland and July’s four fatal crashes, and the pattern is hard to miss.

"what little effort went into the report"?

I disagree, a lot of effort went in to minimize the report, to portray it as an unremarkable accident.

That is the effort I find Tesla criminally responsible for.

Recent findings suggest that the CHP need the full report, no redactions. If they chose to censor it that is their task, not Tesla's.

Sources indicate that what stands out in this one is how little effort went into the report. Tesla knows the speed, knows the system was on, and has telematics. But it couldn’t fill in what the car hit, and it learned about three deaths in one of its cars from the news. Then it redacted the one field, the narrative, that would tell us what the car did.

Industry observers note that tesla wants regulators and customers to trust FSD with no one watching. That trust has to be earned with data. A firm that seals the account of what its car did at 74 mph in a neighborhood, in a crash that killed three people, isn’t earning it.

Sources indicate that we’re asking CHP Placerville whether its investigators knew the system was engaged, whether they got Tesla’s raw data or Tesla’s summary of it, and what they found about the fire and the doors. If CHP never got the full data, how will it ever determine the cause?

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, THERE COMES A time in every man’s life—sans the few genetically gifted—when he must face hair loss. It hits sooner than many expect, as the American Hair Loss Association notes that 85 percent of men will face hair loss by age 50. There are then two options: lean into it and join the Stanley Tucci Gang, or invest in equipment to regrow hair. For the latter, the best tools to reverse balding at home are laser hair growth devices.

According to recent reports, the majority of men lose their hair due to male pattern baldness (also known as androgenetic alopecia), a condition caused by genetic predisposition and hormonal influences, wherein testosterone is declining and dihydrotestosterone (aka DHT) is surging. This process is characterized by the classic receding hairline look, along with thinning around the crown.

Laser hair growth devices are best at treating this cause of hair loss, explains dermatologist and founder of Remedy, Dr. Muneeb Shah, MD. Other common factors like stress, illness, medications, nutritional deficiencies, and autoimmune diseases will be less responsive to laser therapies, as hair follicles are often damaged or inactive from these issues and less willing to be rebooted from light treatment.

According to recent reports, laser hair growth devices work by using low-level laser therapy, or LLLT, to stimulate weakened or dormant hair follicles, says hair restoration physician and creator of the Bauman Turbo LaserCap, Dr. Alan Bauman, MD. The process is known as photobiomodulation, and it involves exposing tissues to light in the red and near-infrared spectrum, which can improve cell metabolism and blood flow, reduce inflammation, and stimulate hair follicles to re-enter and maintain the growth phase.

In a recent development, generally, LLLT does not include LED; instead, it uses laser diodes. However, some devices will combine both for added effectiveness or to reduce the intensity of laser diodes. “In simpler terms, laser therapy supercharges the environment for healthy hair growth by restoring energy to sluggish follicles and optimizing scalp conditions,” Dr. Bauman claims.

Laser hair growth devices are rarely cheap (you won’t find an effective one below $400), so you want to make sure you’re getting the right option for you before making the investment. After chatting with the pros, these are the five laser hair growth devices worth considering.

Industry observers note that the biggest dilemma when buying a laser hair growth device is choosing between LED and laser diodes, but with the iRestore Laser Therapy Hair Growth System, you don’t have to. This device uses a hybrid of laser diodes and LEDs to get the best of both worlds, pairing the gentle nature of LEDs with the power of laser diodes. Dr. Shah backs it, noting that iRestore is reputable and the device is FDA-cleared.

While results will be stronger closer to 650 or 660 nanometers, this range is powerful enough to reduce inflammation, decrease DHT levels (to maintain follicle strength), and improve blood flow on the scalp (to provide hair follicles with more oxygen and nutrients needed for growth).

Sources indicate that men’s Health writer Bob Gearing wore the HigherDose Red Light Therapy Hat every day for the past year, and swears by the results. He notes that this nifty cap is both more effective than Rogaine and less invasive, leaving no irritation or redness. It’s super easy to use, pop it on like any hat, and wear for 10 minutes a day while the 650 nanometer LED red light penetrates the scalp to promote a healthier environment for hair growth.

The brand lists 16 months as the target, but the best results will appear after six months. Unlike the Capillus cap, whose red light peaks through the sides during use, this is the only hair growth device you could get away with wearing in public without anyone noticing. It simply looks like a black hat, nothing more. This makes it both easy to use and even easier to incorporate into your daily routine.

Sources indicate that as Dr. Bauman puts it, not all laser hair growth devices are created equal. The first thing to consider is what light is being used in your device to stimulate growth. The two primary options are LEDs (Light Emitting Diodes) and laser diodes. He recommends zeroing in on laser diodes as they’re more powerful and penetrate deeper into the scalp, targeting the hair follicle root more effectively.

From a strict regrowth perspective, laser diodes will be more effective; however, these also present more potential side effects given their strength, such as hyperpigmentation, burns, redness, and swelling. LEDs present fewer side effects, so they’re better for sensitive scalps, but they won’t penetrate the scalp and hair follicles as deeply. This means LED is best suited for early shedding and will struggle to help more severe hair loss.

For both LED and laser diode options, the therapeutic wavelength is crucial. Dr. Shah recommends wavelengths between 630 and 680 nanometers to successfully penetrate the scalp and stimulate hair follicle growth. If you have sensitive skin or are latest to these tools, take it slow and work your way to the top level to limit irritation.

It has been revealed that dr. Bauman says that the 650-nanometer range is key, as it is the optimal wavelength absorbed by mitochondria for energy production to support hair follicle function. This process boosts cellular energy, as hair follicles are highly active structures that need a lot of energy to support the hair growth cycle. The end result is reduced inflammation, improved blood flow, and extended growth.

To be clear, no laser hair growth device is going to give you Thor-level flow overnight—these tools take time. Dr. Shah says that men will need at least six months of consistent use before seeing results after regular use. But not every device’s session will be the same. Some, you’ll need to wear or place near the dome for five minutes, while others for half an hour. Consider the comfort of your device, along with your schedule, before investing.

Recent findings suggest that most importantly, however, Dr. Shah states consistency is crucial because missing sessions, no matter how long they are, can reduce the device’s effectiveness. If executed properly, early results will appear around six months, such as reduced shedding or slight thickening, before fuller regrowth occurs near the one-year mark, according to Dr. Shah.

Whenever you’re dealing with newly introduced technology, rely on reputable organizations to first approve it for use. Both Dr. Shah and Dr. Bauman advise only looking to laser hair growth devices that have been accepted by the FDA for the safest, most effective experience. However, there are different levels of FDA acceptance. FDA-listed or FDA-registered simply means that the manufacturer has informed the FDA, but doesn’t imply approval or authorization.

FDA clearance, on the other hand, means the device is substantially equivalent to a product already on the market.

Industry observers note that FDA approved is the ideal, as this means the device has successfully been through extensive testing and clinical trials to demonstrate safety and effectiveness. But to date, there have been no LED or laser diode devices for hair growth that are FDA-approved, so look for FDA-cleared options.

As someone whose hairline is still going strong after 33 years (and a ton of preventive hair thinning products), I leaned heavily on the counsel of hair loss professionals for these selections. I conferred with dermatologist Dr. Shah and hair restoration physician Dr. Bauman on what to look for in an effective laser hair growth device and which they recommend.

Sources indicate that I also consulted with fellow Men’s Health writers and editors who have battled hair loss on their experience, based on ease of use, effectiveness, and long-term results.
